To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the history dependence of odor-triggered flight decisions is consistent with a model in which the animal accumulates information about the plume center-line over time.

the flight trajectories of flying insects navigating in turbulent plumes of attractive odors are modulated by the concentration of the odors encountered, and by the order in which they are encountered, with the latter history dependence being consistent with a model in which the animal is accumulating information about the source location over time.
history dependence in insect flight during odor tracking is consistent with a strategy that maximizes expected information gain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of natural decision-making in complex and variable environments.
understanding the mechanisms by which animals make decisions and how these decisions change in response to their environment and previous experiences.
the problem of how animals navigate in complex, turbulent, and variable environments, in particular, in odor plumes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
history-dependent modulation of decision sequences is a general phenomenon that may be relevant to many natural navigation scenarios.
the observed history dependence of odor-triggered turns in Drosophila and Aedes is consistent with a model of information-based decision making, but is not conclusive evidence for this model.
history dependence in insect plume tracking is consistent with the accumulation and use of information about the plume source.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
history dependence is a common feature of natural decision sequences, and that this feature may reflect the accumulation of information over time.
history dependence is an important feature of insect odor tracking, and that it is consistent with the idea that insects are using information about the plume structure to make flight decisions.
we show how the dynamics of natural decision-making can be decomposed into a reactive response and a memory-based modulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the study of natural decision-making can be advanced by the development of normative models that incorporate the structure of the decision-making environment.
even in a simple scenario like odor tracking, the dynamics of decision sequences are richly structured and difficult to predict from the statistics of individual decisions.
even simple, short-term decision-making can involve complex history dependence that depends on the details of the task.
